segments.text: Most people think of AI like a search engine.
You type in one perfect prompt and you expect one perfect finalized answer in return.
Instead, picture your interaction with AI as a two-person group project.
The group is small, just you and the AI, working together.
Your best work won't come from a single command.
It requires a back-and-forth conversation where both of you share ideas,
figure out what is missing, and actively improve the project together.
The first collaborative move is to use AI as a thought partner.
You exchange questions and bounce ideas off each other, though you always make the final decisions.
Looking at this board for starting a summer business,
you can begin the conversation on the right by saying,
I'd like to earn money this summer by starting a small business.
Can we talk through what might fit me?
The AI doesn't immediately give you a generic list.
It counters with a question of its own.
What are you already good at?
And what problems do people around you regularly need help solving?
You reply with your specific skills,
noting that you are good with dogs and teaching younger kids math.
The AI synthesizes those precise skills into three realistic business directions.
It then asks you to choose which option sounds most interesting and easiest to start.
A good conversation asks about you before it answers.
The second move is using AI as a learning tool.
When a concept is confusing, you can ask the AI to explain it,
connect the idea to something familiar and check your understanding.
In this example, the user asks the AI to explain the concept of profit.
Specifically, they ask it to use simple numbers that apply to a lawn mowing business.
The AI responds with a direct definition.
Profit is the money left after you subtract every cost from your sales.
Looking at the equation at the bottom, the AI breaks it down exactly.
For example, your sales are $300.
Your total costs are $150, leaving you with $150 in profit.
The formula is sales minus costs equals profit.
Ask AI to explain the idea using a situation you know.
Sometimes you face a massive decision, like planning for college,
and you don't even know where to begin.
AI can help you overcome that paralysis.
On this board, the user gives a strict instruction.
I need to start thinking about college, but I don't know where to begin.
Ask me one question at a time to help me figure out what matters to me.
Don't recommend a college yet.
The AI honors that constraint, providing a foundational starting question to determine priorities.
Do you already have a career or field in mind,
or do you want college to help you explore different possibilities?
When you don't know where to begin, ask AI for the first question.
The final move is working with AI over several rounds.
To iterate means to build something in versions,
using each version to improve the next.
This board shows the difference iteration makes.
In the early round on the left, a vague request for summer business ideas
yields a generic, unhelpful list.
In a later round, the user defines tight parameters.
They specify a lawn cutting business serving homes within biking distance,
using the customer's mower, working weekday afternoons, and charging by lawn size.
They then ask the AI to find weaknesses in the plan.
The AI uses those precise constraints to pressure test the logistics,
asking how will you quote lawn sizes and what happens when it rains?
Better details give AI better material to improve.
The next level starts after the first answer.
Explore ideas, build understanding, and improve together.
